quotes.text: To be angry with a man is to hate him; to hate him is to wish him harm; but to wish him well, even if he has done you harm, is the mark of a great mind.
quotes.cite: Seneca, On Anger (De Ira) 2.34.5 (translated by John W. Basore)

quotes.text: Do you seek Alcides' equal? None is, except himself.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Once again prosperous and successful crime goes by the name of virtue; good men obey the bad, might is right and fear oppresses law.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: He [Hercules] will find a way — or make one.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Unrighteous fortune seldom spares the highest worth; no one with safety can long front so frequent perils. Whom calamity oft passes by she finds at last.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Who vaunts his race, lauds what belongs to others.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Tis the first art of kings, the power to suffer hate.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Arms observe no bounds; nor can the wrath of the sword, once drawn, be easily checked or stayed; war delights in blood.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Of war men ask the outcome, not the cause.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Who can be forced has not learned how to die.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: No easy way leads from the earth to heaven..
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: Things ’twas hard to bear ’tis pleasant to recall.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Hercules Furens (The Madness of Hercules)

quotes.text: He who, when he may, forbids not sin, commands it.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Troades (The Trojan Women)

quotes.text: Mercy oft doth offer death, not life.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Troades (The Trojan Women)

quotes.text: Pyrrhus: No law the wretched captive's life doth spare. Agamemnon: What law forbids not, let this shame forbid. Pyrrhus: 'Tis victor's right to do whate'er he will. Pyrrhus: Then should he will the least who most can do.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Troades (The Trojan Women)

quotes.text: Small the grief is that can counsel take.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Medea

quotes.text: The man who hopes for naught at least has naught to fear.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Medea

quotes.text: Unrighteous sovereignty has never long endured.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Medea

quotes.text: Light cares speak out, the weighty have no words.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Phaedra

quotes.text: Alternate translation: One crime has to be concealed by another.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Phaedra

quotes.text: Not circumstance but will can make impure.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Phaedra

quotes.text: Tis the upright mind that holds true sovereignty.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Thyestes

quotes.text: On him does death lie heavily, who, but too well known to all, dies to himself unknown.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Thyestes

quotes.text: Worse than war is the very fear of war.
quotes.section: Tragedies › Thyestes

quotes.text: What man can you show me who places any value on his time, who reckons the worth of each day, who understands that he is dying daily?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter I: On Saving Time

quotes.text: For we are mistaken when we look forward to death; the major portion of death has already passed. Whatever years be behind us are in death's hands.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter I: On Saving Time

quotes.text: Lay hold of today’s task, and you will not need to depend so much upon tomorrow’s. While we are postponing, life speeds by.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter I: On Saving Time

quotes.text: It is too late to spare when you reach the dregs of the cask.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter I: On Saving Time

quotes.text: The primary indication, to my thinking, of a well-ordered mind is a man’s ability to remain in one place and linger in his own company.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter II: On discursiveness in reading

quotes.text: Who is everywhere is nowhere. When a person spends all his time in foreign travel, he ends by having many acquaintances, but no friends.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter II: On discursiveness in reading

quotes.text: It is not the man who has too little, but the man who craves more, that is poor.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter II: On discursiveness in reading

quotes.text: For love of bustle is not industry – it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter III: On true and false friendship

quotes.text: No man can have a peaceful life who thinks too much about lengthening it.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter IV: On the terrors of death

quotes.text: Most men ebb and flow in wretchedness between the fear of death and the hardships of life; they are unwilling to live, and yet they do not know how to die.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter IV: On the terrors of death

quotes.text: No man has ever been so far advanced by Fortune that she did not threaten him as greatly as she had previously indulged him.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter IV: On the terrors of death

quotes.text: I commend you and rejoice in the fact that you are persistent in your studies, and that, putting all else aside, you make it each day your endeavour to become a better man.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter V: On the Philosopher’s Mean

quotes.text: Of course, however, the living voice and the intimacy of a common life will help you more than the written word. You must go to the scene of action, first, because men put more faith in their eyes than in their ears, and second, because the way is long if one follows precepts, but short and helpful, if one follows patterns.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter VI: On precepts and exemplars

quotes.text: What progress, you ask, have I made? I have begun to be a friend to myself.” That was indeed a great benefit; such a person can never be alone. You may be sure that such a man is a friend to all mankind.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter VI: On precepts and exemplars

quotes.text: But both courses are to be avoided; you should not copy the bad simply because they are many, nor should you hate the many because they are unlike you.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter VII: On crowds

quotes.text: Withdraw into yourself, as far as you can. Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve. The process is mutual; for men learn while they teach.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter VII: On crowds

quotes.text: Live among men as if God beheld you; speak with God as if men were listening.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter X: On living to oneself

quotes.text: The best ideas are common property.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XII: On old age

quotes.text: ... the only contestant who can confidently enter the lists is the man who has seen his own blood, who has felt his teeth rattle beneath his opponent’s fist, who has been tripped and felt the full force of his adversary’s charge, who has been downed in body but not in spirit, one who, as often as he falls, rises again with greater defiance than ever.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XIII: On Groundless Fears

quotes.text: Let another say. “Perhaps the worst will not happen.” You yourself must say. “Well, what if it does happen? Let us see who wins! Perhaps it happens for my best interests; it may be that such a death will shed credit upon my life.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XIII: On Groundless Fears

quotes.text: Socrates was ennobled by the hemlock draught. Wrench from Cato's hand his sword, the vindicator of liberty, and you deprive him of the greatest share of his glory.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XIII: On Groundless Fears

quotes.text: There are more things, Lucilius, likely to frighten us than there are to crush us; we suffer more often in imagination than in reality.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XIII: On Groundless Fears

quotes.text: The old Romans had a custom which survived even into my lifetime. They would add to the opening words of a letter: "If you are well, it is well; I also am well." Persons like ourselves would do well to say. "If you are studying philosophy, it is well." For this is just what "being well" means. Without philosophy the mind is sickly.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XV

quotes.text: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy—no, nor even actual want. For when hastening after wisdom, we must endure even hunger. Men have endured hunger when their towns were besieged, and what other reward for their endurance did they obtain than that they did not fall under the conqueror’s power? How much greater is the promise of the prize of everlasting liberty, and the assurance that we need fear neither God nor man! Even though we starve, we must reach that goal.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XVII: On Philosophy and Riches

quotes.text: Armies have endured all manner of want, have lived on roots, and have resisted hunger by means of food too revolting to mention. All this they have suffered to gain a kingdom, and—what is more marvellous—to gain a kingdom that will be another’s. Will any man hesitate to endure poverty, in order that he may free his mind from madness?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XVII: On Philosophy and Riches

quotes.text: If you would not have a man flinch when the crisis comes, train him before it comes.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XVIII: On Festivals and Fasting

quotes.text: A trifling debt makes a man your debtor; a large one makes him an enemy.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XIX: On worldliness and retirement

quotes.text: Prove your words by your deeds.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XX: On practicing what you preach

quotes.text: What is wisdom? Always desiring the same things, and always refusing the same things.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XX: On practicing what you preach

quotes.text: Press on, therefore, as you have begun; perhaps you will be led to perfection, or to a point which you alone understand is still short of perfection.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XX: On practicing what you preach

quotes.text: Men do not care how nobly they live, but only how long, although it is within the reach of every man to live nobly, but within no man's power to live long.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXII: On the futility of half-way measures

quotes.text: It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: You will thus understand that what you fear is either insignificant or short-lived.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: Mucius put his hand into the fire. It is painful to be burned; but how much more painful to inflict such suffering upon oneself!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: [Mucius] might have accomplished something more successful in that camp, but never anything more brave.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: It was a great deed to conquer Carthage, but a greater deed to conquer death.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: Remember, however, before all else, to strip things of all that disturbs and confuses, and to see what each is at bottom; you will then comprehend that they contain nothing fearful except the actual fear.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXIV: On despising death

quotes.text: I may become a poor man; I shall then be one among many. I may be exiled; I shall then regard myself as born in the place to which I shall be sent. They may put me in chains. What then? Am I free from bonds now? Behold this clogging burden of a body, to which nature has fettered me! “I shall die,” you say; you mean to say “I shall cease to run the risk of sickness; I shall cease to run the risk of imprisonment; I shall cease to run the risk of death.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXV: On Reformation

quotes.text: I do not know whether I shall make progress; but I should prefer to lack success rather than to lack faith.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXV: On Reformation

quotes.text: You do not know where death awaits you; so be ready for it everywhere.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVI: On Old Age and Death

quotes.text: What," say you, "are you giving me advice? Indeed, have you already advised yourself, already corrected your own faults? Is this the reason why you have leisure to reform other men?" No, I am not so shameless as to undertake to cure my fellow-men when I am ill myself. I am, however, discussing with you troubles which concern us both, and sharing the remedy with you, just as if we were lying ill in the same hospital.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVII

quotes.text: Virtue alone affords everlasting and peace-giving joy; even if some obstacle arise, it is but like an intervening cloud, which floats beneath the sun but never prevails against it.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVII

quotes.text: You need a change of soul rather than a change of climate.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

quotes.text: You must lay aside the burdens of the mind; until you do this, no place will satisfy you.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

quotes.text: If one doesn't know his mistakes, he won't want to correct them.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXVIII: On travel as a cure for discontent

quotes.text: A great pilot can sail even when his canvas is rent.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXX: On conquering the conqueror

quotes.text: He who does not wish to die cannot have wished to live.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXX: On conquering the conqueror

quotes.text: I forbid you to be cast down or depressed. It is not enough if you do not shrink from work; ask for it.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXI: On Siren Songs

quotes.text: Would you know what makes men greedy for the future? It is because no one has yet found himself.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXII: On Progress

quotes.text: Besides, he who follows another not only discovers nothing but is not even investigating.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXIII

quotes.text: What then? Shall I not follow in the footsteps of my predecessors? I shall indeed use the old road, but if I find one that makes a shorter cut and is smoother to travel, I shall open the new road. Men who have made these discoveries before us are not our masters, but our guides. Truth lies open for all; it has not yet been monopolized. And there is plenty of it left even for posterity to discover.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXIII

quotes.text: Friendship is always helpful, but love sometimes even does harm
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXV

quotes.text: You must die erect and unyielding.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXVII: On Allegiance to Virtue

quotes.text: It is disgraceful, instead of proceeding ahead, to be carried along, and then suddenly, amid the whirlpool of events, to ask in a dazed way: “How did I get into this condition?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXVII: On Allegiance to Virtue

quotes.text: It is the quality of a great soul to scorn great things and to prefer that which is ordinary rather than that which is too great.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXIX: On Noble Aspirations

quotes.text: Then it is that the height of unhappiness is reached, when men are not only attracted, but even pleased, by shameful things, and when there is no longer any room for a cure, now that those things which once were vices have become habits.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XXXIX: On Noble Aspirations

quotes.text: You are doing an excellent thing, one which will be wholesome for you, if, as you write me, you are persisting in your effort to attain sound understanding; it is foolish to pray for this when you can acquire it from yourself. We do not need to uplift our hands towards heaven, or to beg the keeper of a temple to let us approach his idol's ear, as if in this way our prayers were more likely to be heard. A god is near you, with you, and in you. This is what I mean, Lucilius: there sits a holy spirit within us, one who marks our good and bad deeds, and is our a guardian.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLI: On the god within us

quotes.text: If you see a man who is unterrified in the midst of dangers, untouched by desires, happy in adversity, peaceful amid the storm, who looks down upon men from a higher plane, and views the gods on a footing of equality, will not a feeling of reverence for him steal over you, will you not say: “This quality is too great and too lofty to be regarded as resembling this petty body in which it dwells? A divine power has descended upon that man.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLI: On the god within us

quotes.text: No man ought to glory except in that which is his own.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLI: On the god within us

quotes.text: Very often the things that cost nothing cost us the most heavily; I can show you many objects the quest and acquisition of which have wrested freedom from our hands.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLII: On Values

quotes.text: You will have less money.” Yes, and less trouble. “Less influence.” Yes, and less envy.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLII: On Values

quotes.text: He that owns himself has lost nothing. But how few men are blessed with ownership of self!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLII: On Values

quotes.text: It is quality rather than quantity that matters.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLV: On sophistical argumentation

quotes.text: They are slaves,” people declare. Nay, rather they are men. “Slaves!” No, comrades. “Slaves!” No, they are unpretentious friends. “Slaves!” No, they are our fellow-slaves, if one reflects that Fortune has equal rights over slaves and free men alike.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: Kindly remember that he whom you call your slave sprang from the same stock, is smiled upon by the same skies, and on equal terms with yourself breathes, lives and dies. It is just as possible for you to see in him a free-born man as for him to see in you a slave.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: Treat your inferiors as you would be treated by your betters.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: I propose to value them according to their character, and not according to their duties. Each man acquires his character for himself, but accident assigns his duties.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: He is a slave.” His soul, however, may be that of a freeman. “He is a slave.” But shall that stand in his way? Show me a man who is not a slave; one is a slave to lust, another to greed, another to ambition, and all men are slaves to fear.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: Would you really know what philosophy offers to humanity? Philosophy offers counsel.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLVII: On master and slave

quotes.text: Show me that the good in life does not depend upon life’s length, but upon the use we make of it; also, that it is possible, or rather usual, for a man who has lived long to have lived too little. Say to me when I lie down to sleep: “You may not wake again!” And when I have waked: “You may not go to sleep again!” Say to me when I go forth from my house: “You may not return!” And when I return: “You may never go forth again!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XLIX: On the Shortness of Life

quotes.text: For what else are you busied with except improving yourself every day, laying aside some error, and coming to understand that the faults which you attribute to circumstances are in yourself?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter L: On Our Blindness and Its Cure

quotes.text: And what is freedom, you ask? It means not being a slave to any circumstance, to any constraint, to any chance; it means compelling Fortune to enter the lists on equal terms.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LI: On Baiae and Morals

quotes.text: Would not anyone who is a man have his slumbers broken by a war-trumpet rather than by a chorus of serenaders?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LI: On Baiae and Morals

quotes.text: You can tell the character of every man when you see how he gives and receives praise.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LII: On choosing our teachers

quotes.text: Our luxuries have condemned us to weakness; we have ceased to be able to do that which we have long declined to do.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LV: On Vatia’s Villa

quotes.text: The much occupied man has no time for wantonness, and it is an obvious commonplace that the evils of leisure can be shaken off by hard work.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LVI: On quiet and study

quotes.text: We are weak, watery beings standing in the midst of unrealities; therefore let us turn our minds to the things that are everlasting.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LVIII: On Being

quotes.text: But the wise man is fortified against all inroads; he is alert; he will not retreat before the attack of poverty, or of sorrow, or of disgrace, or of pain. He will walk undaunted both against them and among them.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LIX: On Pleasure and Joy

quotes.text: The wise man is joyful, happy and calm, unshaken, he lives on a plane with the gods.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LIX: On Pleasure and Joy

quotes.text: That which Fortune has not given, she cannot take away.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LIX: On Pleasure and Joy

quotes.text: I am endeavouring to live every day as if it were a complete life.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXI: On meeting death cheerfully

quotes.text: Before I became old I tried to live well; now that I am old, I shall try to die well; but dying well means dying gladly.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXI: On meeting death cheerfully

quotes.text: The shortest way to wealth is through the contempt of wealth.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXII

quotes.text: Fortune has taken away, but Fortune has given.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXIII

quotes.text: Let us greedily enjoy our friends, because we do not know how long this privilege will be ours.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXIII

quotes.text: Whatever can happen at any time can happen today.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXIII

quotes.text: All art is but imitation of nature.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXV: On the first cause

quotes.text: Great also are the souls of the defenders—men who know that, as long as the path to death lies open, the blockade is not complete, men who breathe their last in the arms of liberty.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVI: On Various Aspects of Virtue

quotes.text: Allow me, excellent Lucilius, to utter a still bolder word: if any goods could be greater than others, I should prefer those which seem harsh to those which are mild and alluring, and should pronounce them greater. For it is more of an accomplishment to break one’s way through difficulties than to keep joy within bounds.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVI: On Various Aspects of Virtue

quotes.text: There stood Mucius, despising the enemy and despising the fire, and watched his hand as it dripped blood over the fire on his enemy’s altar, until Porsenna, envying the fame of the hero whose punishment he was advocating, ordered the fire to be removed against the will of the victim.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVI: On Various Aspects of Virtue

quotes.text: I cannot help believing that Mucius was all the more lucky because he manipulated the flames as calmly as if he were holding out his hand to the manipulator. He had wiped out all his previous mistakes; he finished the war unarmed and maimed; and with that stump of a hand he conquered two kings.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVI: On Various Aspects of Virtue

quotes.text: I should prefer to be free from torture; but if the time comes when it must be endured, I shall desire that I may conduct myself therein with bravery, honour, and courage. Of course I prefer that war should not occur; but if war does occur, I shall desire that I may nobly endure the wounds, the starvation, and all that the exigency of war brings. Nor am I so mad as to crave illness; but if I must suffer illness, I shall desire that I may do nothing which shows lack of restraint, and nothing that is unmanly. The conclusion is, not that hardships are desirable, but that virtue is desirable, which enables us patiently to endure hardships.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVII: On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering

quotes.text: Now a life of honour includes various kinds of conduct; it may include the chest in which Regulus was confined, or the wound of Cato which was torn open by Cato’s own hand, or the exile of Rutilius, or the cup of poison which removed Socrates from gaol to heaven.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVII: On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering

quotes.text: Clothe yourself with a hero’s courage, and withdraw for a little space from the opinions of the common man. Form a proper conception of the image of virtue, a thing of exceeding beauty and grandeur; this image is not to be worshipped by us with incense or garlands, but with sweat and blood.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVII: On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering

quotes.text: I should prefer that Fortune keep me in her camp rather than in the lap of luxury. If I am tortured, but bear it bravely, all is well; if I die, but die bravely, it is also well.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVII: On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering

quotes.text: Why should I not regard this as desirable—not because the fire, burns me, but because it does not overcome me?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXVII: On Ill-Health and Endurance of Suffering

quotes.text: The wise man will live as long as he ought, not as long as he can.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXX: On the proper time to slip the cable

quotes.text: Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXI: On the supreme good

quotes.text: The archer must know what he is seeking to hit; then he must aim and control the weapon by his skill. Our plans miscarry because they have no aim. When a man does not know what harbour he is making for, no wind is the right wind. Chance must necessarily have great influence over our lives, because we live by chance. It is the case with certain men, however, that they do not know that they know certain things. Just as we often go searching for those who stand beside us, so we are apt to forget that the goal of the Supreme Good lies near us.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXI: On the supreme good

quotes.text: These actions are not essentially difficult; it is we ourselves that are soft and flabby.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXI: On the supreme good

quotes.text: He knows his own strength; he knows that he was born to carry burdens.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXI: On the supreme good

quotes.text: Do you ask me whom I have conquered? Neither the Persians, nor the far-off Medes, nor any warlike race that lies beyond the Dahae; not these, but greed, ambition, and the fear of death that has conquered the conquerors of the world.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXI: On the supreme good

quotes.text: But no wall can be erected against Fortune which she cannot take by storm; let us strengthen our inner defences. If the inner part be safe, man can be attacked, but never captured.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXIV: On Virtue as a Refuge From Worldly Distractions

quotes.text: But the wise man knows that all things are in store for him. Whatever happens, he says: “I knew it.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVI: On Learning Wisdom in Old Age

quotes.text: As long as you live, keep learning how to live.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVI: On Learning Wisdom in Old Age

quotes.text: There are times when we ought to die and are unwilling; sometimes we die and are unwilling.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVII: On Taking One’s Own Life

quotes.text: Would you not think him an utter fool who wept because he was not alive a thousand years ago? And is he not just as much of a fool who weeps because he will not be alive a thousand years from now? It is all the same; you will not be, and you were not. Neither of these periods of time belongs to you.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVII: On Taking One’s Own Life

quotes.text: So near at hand is freedom, and is anyone still a slave?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVII: On Taking One’s Own Life

quotes.text: What else is there which you would regret to have taken from you? Friends? But who can be a friend to you? Country? What? Do you think enough of your country to be late to dinner? The light of the sun? You would extinguish it, if you could; for what have you ever done that was fit to be seen in the light?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVII: On Taking One’s Own Life

quotes.text: For sometimes it is an act of bravery even to live.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind
quotes.cite: Seneca, Ad Lucilium epistulae morales, transl. Richard M. Gummere, 1920 ed., Epistle LXXVIII, pp. 181-182

quotes.text: There is no sorrow in the world, when we have escaped from the fear of death.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: You will die, not because you are ill, but because you are alive; even when you have been cured, thesame end awaits you; when you have recovered, it will be not death, but ill health, that you have escaped.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: No man can suffer both severely and for a long time; Nature, who loves us most tenderly, has so constituted us as to make pain either endurable or short.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: It is nothing—a trifling matter at most; keep a stout heart and it will soon cease”; then in thinking it slight, you will make it slight. Everything depends on opinion; ambition, luxury, greed, hark back to opinion. It is according to opinion that we suffer.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: Two elements must therefore be rooted out once for all—the fear of future suffering, and the recollection of past suffering; since the latter no longer concerns me, and the former concerns me not yet.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: Is it for this purpose that we are strong—that we may have light burdens to bear?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: Meanwhile, hold fast to this thought, and grip it close: yield not to adversity; trust not to prosperity; keep before your eyes the full scope of Fortune’s power, as if she would surely do whatever is in her power to do.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXVIII: On the Healing Power of the Mind

quotes.text: Our feeling about every obligation depends in each case upon the spirit in which the benefit is conferred; we weigh not the bulk of the gift, but the quality of the good-will which prompted it.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXI: On benefits

quotes.text: My master Attalus used to say: "Evil herself drinks the largest portion of her own poison." The poison which serpents carry for the destruction of others, and secrete without harm to themselves, is not like this poison; for this sort is ruinous to the possessor.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXI: On benefits

quotes.text: You must go now, fellow-soldiers, to yonder place, whence there is no ‘must’ about your returning!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXII: On the Natural Fear of Death

quotes.text: Drunkenness is nothing but voluntary madness.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXIII: On Drunkenness

quotes.text: It is a rough road that leads to the heights of greatness.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXIV: On gathering ideas

quotes.text: But he has no fear; unconquered he looks down from a lofty height upon his sufferings.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXV: On Some Vain Syllogisms

quotes.text: Thus no fortune, no external circumstance, can shut off the wise man from action. For the very thing which engages his attention prevents him from attending to other things. He is ready for either outcome: if it brings goods, he controls them; if evils, he conquers them.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXV: On Some Vain Syllogisms

quotes.text: So the wise man will develop virtue, if he may, in the midst of wealth, or, if not, in poverty; if possible, in his own country—if not, in exile; if possible, as a commander—if not, as a common soldier; if possible, in sound health—if not, enfeebled. Whatever fortune he finds, he will accomplish therefrom something noteworthy.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXV: On Some Vain Syllogisms

quotes.text: A sword by itself does not slay; it is merely the weapon used by the slayer.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXVII: Some arguments in favor of the simple life

quotes.text: It is better, of course, to know useless things than to know nothing.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXVIII: On liberal and vocational studies

quotes.text: Just as an enemy is more dangerous to a retreating army, so every trouble that fortune brings attacks us all the harder if we yield and turn our backs.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter LXXXVIII: On liberal and vocational studies

quotes.text: It would be some consolation for the feebleness of our selves and our works, if all things should perish as slowly as they come into being; but as it is, increases are of sluggish growth, but the way to ruin is rapid.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCI: On the Lesson to be Drawn From the Burning of Lyons

quotes.text: Perhaps its destruction has been brought about only that it may be raised up again to a better destiny. Oftentimes a reverse has but made room for more prosperous fortune. Many structures have fallen only to rise to a greater height.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCI: On the Lesson to be Drawn From the Burning of Lyons

quotes.text: Alexander, king of Macedon, began to study geometry; unhappy man, because he would thereby learn how puny was that earth of which he had seized but a fraction! Unhappy man, I repeat, because he was bound to understand that he was bearing a false title. For who can be “great” in that which is puny?
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCI: On the Lesson to be Drawn From the Burning of Lyons

quotes.text: Imagine that nature is saying to us: “Those things of which you complain are the same for all. I cannot give anything easier to any man, but whoever wishes will make things easier for himself.” In what way? By equanimity. You must suffer pain, and thirst, and hunger, and old age too, if a longer stay among men shall be granted you; you must be sick, and you must suffer loss and death.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCI: On the Lesson to be Drawn From the Burning of Lyons

quotes.text: That man, I declare, is happy whom nothing makes less strong than he is; he keeps to the heights, leaning upon none but himself; for one who sustains himself by any prop may fall.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCII: On the Happy Life

quotes.text: For no man is free who is a slave to his body.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCII: On the Happy Life

quotes.text: Don't ask for what you'll wish you hadn't got.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCV: On the usefulness of basic principles

quotes.text: We often want one thing and pray for another, not telling the truth even to the gods.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCV: On the usefulness of basic principles

quotes.text: As our acts and our thoughts are, so will our lives be.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCV: On the usefulness of basic principles

quotes.text: And yet life, Lucilius, is really a battle.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCVI

quotes.text: For this reason those who are tossed about at sea, who proceed uphill and downhill over toilsome crags and heights, who go on campaigns that bring the greatest danger, are heroes and front-rank fighters; but persons who live in rotten luxury and ease while others toil, are mere turtle-doves safe only because men despise them.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCVI

quotes.text: All the Good of mortals is mortal.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCVIII: On the Fickleness of Fortune

quotes.text: Of all these experiences that seem so frightful, none is insuperable. Separate trials have been over- come by many: fire by Mucius, crucifixion by Regulus, poison by Socrates, exile by Rutilius, and a sword-inflicted death by Cato; therefore, let us also overcome something.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCVIII: On the Fickleness of Fortune

quotes.text: Whoever complains about the death of anyone, is complaining that he was a man. Everyone is bound by the same terms: he who is privileged to be born, is destined to die.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCIX: On Consolation to the Bereaved

quotes.text: Accept in an unruffled spirit that which is inevitable.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter XCIX: On Consolation to the Bereaved

quotes.text: But how foolish it is to set out one’s life, when one is not even owner of the morrow!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CI: On the Futility of Planning Ahead

quotes.text: The point is, not how long you live, but how nobly you live. And often this living nobly means that you cannot live long.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CI: On the Futility of Planning Ahead

quotes.text: Socrates is reported to have replied, when a certain person complained of having received no benefit from his travels: “It serves you right! You travelled in your own company!
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: What profit is there in crossing the sea and in going from one city to another? If you would escape your troubles, you need not another place but another personality. Perhaps you have reached Athens, or perhaps Rhodes; choose any state you fancy, how does it matter what its character may be? You will be bringing to it your own.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: New friends, however, will not be the same.” No, nor will you yourself remain the same; you change with every day and every hour.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: If you are wise, mingle these two elements: do not hope without despair, or despair without hope.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: This spirit thrusts itself forward, confident of commendation and esteem. It is superior to all, monarch of all it surveys; hence it should be subservient to nothing, finding no task too heavy, and nothing strong enough to weigh down the shoulders of a man.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: But how much more highly do I think of these men! They can do these things, but decline to do them. To whom that ever tried have these tasks proved false? To what man did they not seem easier in the doing? Our lack of confidence is not the result of difficulty. The difficulty comes from our lack of confidence.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: He maintained this attitude up to the very end, and no man ever saw Socrates too much elated or too much depressed. Amid all the disturbance of Fortune, he was undisturbed.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: Do you desire another case? Take that of the younger Marcus Cato, with whom Fortune dealt in a more hostile and more persistent fashion. But he withstood her, on all occasions, and in his last moments, at the point of death, showed that a brave man can live in spite of Fortune, can die in spite of her. His whole life was passed either in civil warfare, or under a political regime which was soon to breed civil war.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: No one ever saw Cato change, no matter how often the state changed: he kept himself the same in all circumstances—in the praetorship, in defeat, under accusation, in his province, on the platform, in the army, in death.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: And this is the vote which [Cato] casts concerning them both: “If Caesar wins, I slay myself; if Pompey, I go into exile.” What was there for a man to fear who, whether in defeat or in victory, had assigned to himself a doom which might have been assigned to him by his enemies in their utmost rage? So he died by his own decision.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: If you set a high value on liberty, you must set a low value on everything else.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CIV: On Care of Health and Peace of Mind

quotes.text: Besides, he who is feared, fears also; no one has been able to arouse terror and live in peace of mind.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CV: On Facing the World With Confidence

quotes.text: Just as we suffer from excess in all things, so we suffer from excess in literature; thus we learn our lessons, not for life, but for the lecture room.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CVI: On the corporeality of virtue

quotes.text: And we cannot change this order of things; but what we can do is to acquire stout hearts, worthy of good men, thereby courageously enduring chance and placing ourselves in harmony with Nature.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CVII: On Obedience to the Universal Will

quotes.text: It is to this law that our souls must adjust themselves, this they should follow, this they should obey. Whatever happens, assume that it was bound to happen, and do not be willing to rail at Nature. That which you cannot reform, it is best to endure, and to attend uncomplainingly upon the God under whose guidance everything progresses; for it is a bad soldier who grumbles when following his commander.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CVII: On Obedience to the Universal Will

quotes.text: They have been spoken by Plato, spoken by Zeno, spoken by Chrysippus or by Posidonius, and by a whole host of Stoics as numerous as excellent. I shall show you how men can prove their words to be their own: it is by doing what they have been talking about.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CVIII: On the Approaches to Philosophy

quotes.text: Let words proceed as they please, provided only your soul keeps its own sure order, provided your soul is great and holds unruffled to its ideals, pleased with itself on account of the very things which displease others, a soul that makes life the test of its progress, and believes that its knowledge is in exact proportion to its freedom from desire and its freedom from fear.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CXV: On the Superficial Blessings

quotes.text: Tell me what to avoid, what to seek, by what studies to strengthen my tottering mind, how I may rebuff the waves that strike me abeam and drive me from my course, by what means I may be able to cope with all my evils, and by what means I can be rid of the calamities that have plunged in upon me and those into which I myself have plunged. Teach me how to bear the burden of sorrow without a groan on my part, and how to bear prosperity without making others groan; also, how to avoid waiting for the ultimate and inevitable end, and to beat a retreat of my own free will, when it seems proper to me to do so.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CXVI: On Real Ethics as Superior to Syllogistic Subtleties

quotes.text: Why then do you occupy me with the words rather than with the works of wisdom? Make me braver, make me calmer, make me the equal of Fortune, make me her superior.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CXVI: On Real Ethics as Superior to Syllogistic Subtleties

quotes.text: I will tell you: that perfect man, who has attained virtue, never cursed his luck, and never received the results of chance with dejection; he believed that he was citizen and soldier of the universe, accepting his tasks as if they were his orders. Whatever happened, he did not spurn it, as if it were evil and borne in upon him by hazard; he accepted it as if it were assigned to be his duty. “Whatever this may be,”he says, “it is my lot; it is rough and it is hard, but I must work diligently at the task.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CXX: More About Virtue

quotes.text: A great step towards independence is a good-humored stomach, one that is willing to endure rough treatment.
quotes.section: Epistulae Morales ad Lucilium (Moral Letters to Lucilius) › Letter CXXIII: On the conflict between pleasure and virtue

quotes.text: The customs of that most criminal nation have gained such strength that they have now been received in all lands. The conquered have given laws to the conquerors.
quotes.section: De Superstitione (On Superstition)
quotes.cite: Apostle Paul: A Polite Bribe by Robert Orlando; p. 108

quotes.text: He who receives a benefit with gratitude, repays the first installment of it.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Beneficiis (On Benefits): Book 2, cap. 22, line 1.

quotes.text: Toward good men God has the mind of a father, he cherishes for them a manly love, and he says, "Let them be harassed by toil, by suffering, by losses, in order that they may gather true strength." Bodies grown fat through sloth are weak, and not only labour, but even movement and their very weight cause them to break down. Unimpaired prosperity cannot withstand a single blow; but he who has struggled constantly with his ills becomes hardened through suffering; and yields to no misfortune; nay, even if he falls, he still fights upon his knees.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Providentia (On Providence), 2.6; translation by John W. Basore

quotes.text: Although," said he [Cato], "all the world has fallen under one man's sway, although Caesar's legions guard the land, his fleets the sea, and Caesar's troops beset the city gates, yet Cato has a way of escape; with one single hand he will open a wide path to freedom. This sword, unstained and blameless even in civil war, shall at last do good and noble service: the freedom which it could not give to his country it shall give to Cato!
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Providentia (On Providence), 2.10; translation by John W. Basore

quotes.text: Why does God afflict the best of men with ill-health, or sorrow, or other troubles? Because in the army the most hazardous services are assigned to the bravest soldiers: a general sends his choicest troops to attack the enemy in a midnight ambuscade, to reconnoitre his line of march, or to drive the hostile garrisons from their strong places. No one of these men says as he begins his march, " The general has dealt hardly with me," but "He has judged well of me.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Providentia (On Providence), 4.8, translated by Aubrey Stewart

quotes.text: De Providentia (On Providence), 5.9, translated by Aubrey Stewart
quotes.section: Moral Essays

quotes.text: We put down mad dogs; we kill the wild, untamed ox; we use the knife on sick sheep to stop their infecting the flock; we destroy abnormal offspring at birth; children, too, if they are born weak or deformed, we drown. Yet this is not the work of anger, but of reason – to separate the sound from the worthless.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 1, cap. 15, line 2 Seneca: Moral and Political Essays (Cambridge UP, 1995) p. 32

quotes.text: A good judge condemns wrongful acts, but does not hate them.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 1, cap. 16, line 6.

quotes.text: No one is able to rule unless he is also able to be ruled.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 15, line 4

quotes.text: The cause of anger is the belief that we are injured; this belief, therefore, should not be lightly entertained. We ought not to fly into a rage even when the injury appears to be open and distinct: for some false things bear the semblance of truth. We should always allow some time to elapse, for time discloses the truth.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 22, line 2

quotes.text: A large part of mankind is angry not with the sins, but with the sinners.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 28, line 8

quotes.text: This is the worst trait of minds rendered arrogant by prosperity, they hate those whom they have injured.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 33, line 6

quotes.text: If any one is angry with you, meet his anger by returning benefits for it: a quarrel which is only taken up on one side falls to the ground: it takes two men to fight.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger): Book 2, cap. 34, line 5.

quotes.text: He who has injured thee was either stronger or weaker than thee. If weaker, spare him; if stronger, spare thyself.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Ira (On Anger); Book III, Chapter V

quotes.text: I do not trust my eyes to tell me what a man is: I have a better and more trustworthy light by which I can distinguish what is true from what is false: let the mind find out what is good for the mind.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Vita Beata (On the Happy Life): cap. 2, line 2

quotes.text: All savageness is a sign of weakness.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Vita Beata (On the Happy Life): cap. 3, line 4

quotes.text: It is not that we have a short space of time, but that we waste much of it. Life is long enough.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Brevitate Vitae ("On the Shortness of Life", trans. John W. Basore), Ch. 1

quotes.text: It is generally agreed that no activity can be successfully pursued by an individual who is preoccupied – not rhetoric or liberal studies – since the mind when distracted absorbs nothing deeply, but rejects everything which is, so to speak, crammed into it.
quotes.section: Moral Essays
quotes.cite: De Brevitate Vitae ("On the Shortness of Life", trans. C. D. N. Costa), Ch. 7

quotes.text: That man lives badly who does not know how to die well.
quotes.section: On Tranquility of the Mind

quotes.text: I shall never be ashamed of citing a bad author if the line is good.
quotes.section: On Tranquility of the Mind

quotes.text: Virtue runs no risk of becoming contemptible by being exposed to view, and it is better to be despised for simplicity than to be tormented by continual hypocrisy.
quotes.section: On Tranquility of the Mind

quotes.text: Our minds must have relaxation: rested, they will rise up better and keener. Just as we must not force fertile fields (for uninterrupted production will quickly exhaust them), so continual labor will break the power of our minds. They will recover their strength, however, after they have had a little freedom and relaxation.
quotes.section: On Tranquility of the Mind

quotes.text: Death is a release from and an end of all pains: beyond it our sufferings cannot extend: it restores us to the peaceful rest in which we lay before we were born. If anyone pities the dead, he ought also to pity those who have not been born. Death is neither a good nor a bad thing, for that alone which is something can be a good or a bad thing: but that which is nothing, and reduces all things to nothing, does not hand us over to either fortune, because good and bad require some material to work upon. Fortune cannot take ahold of that which Nature has let go, nor can a man be unhappy if he is nothing.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: What need is there to weep over parts of life? The whole of it calls for tears.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: By Hercules, the state would have sustained a great loss if you had not brought him forth from the oblivion to which his two splendid qualities, eloquence and independence, had consigned him: he is now read, is popular, is received into men’s hands and bosoms, and fears no old age: but as for those who butchered him, before long men will cease to speak even of their crimes, the only things by which they are remembered.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: All vices sink into our whole being, if we do not crush them before they gain a footing; and in like manner these sad, pitiable, and discordant feelings end by feeding upon their own bitterness, until the unhappy mind takes a sort of morbid delight in grief... In like manner, wounds heal easily when the blood is fresh upon them: they can then be cleared out and brought to the surface, and admit of being probed by the finger: when disease has turned them into malignant ulcers, their cure is more difficult.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: Octavia lost Marcellus, whom both his father-in-law and his uncle had begun to depend upon, and to place upon his shoulders the weight of the empire — a young man of keen intelligence and firm character, frugal and moderate in his desires to an extent which deserved especial admiration in one so young and so wealthy, strong to endure labour, averse to indulgence, and able to bear whatever burden his uncle might choose to lay, or I may say to pile upon his shoulders. Augustus had well chosen him as a foundation, for he would not have given way under any weight, however excessive.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: What madness this is, to punish oneself because one is unfortunate, and not to lessen, but to increase one’s ills! You ought to display, in this matter also, that decent behaviour and modesty which has characterised all your life: for there is such a thing as self-restraint in grief also.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: When we leave you and assemble together by ourselves, we talk freely about his sayings and doings, treating them with the respect which they deserve: in your presence deep silence is observed about him, and thus you lose that greatest of pleasures, the hearing the praises of your son, which I doubt not you would be willing to hand down to all future ages, had you the means of so doing, even at the cost of your own life.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Ad Marciam De Consolatione (To Marcia on Consolation)

quotes.text: You have demanded of me, Novatus, that I should write how anger may be soothed, and it appears to me that you are right in feeling especial fear of this passion, which is above all others hideous and wild: for the others have some alloy of peace and quiet, but this consists wholly in action and the impulse of grief, raging with an utterly inhuman lust for arms, blood and tortures, careless of itself provided it hurts another, rushing upon the very point of the sword, and greedy for revenge even when it drags the avenger to ruin with itself.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Some of the wisest of men have in consequence of this called anger a short madness: for it is equally devoid of self control, regardless of decorum, forgetful of kinship, obstinately engrossed in whatever it begins to do, deaf to reason and advice, excited by trifling causes, awkward at perceiving what is true and just, and very like a falling rock which breaks itself to pieces upon the very thing which it crushes.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: That you may know that they whom anger possesses are not sane, look at their appearance; for as there are distinct symptoms which mark madmen, such as a bold and menacing air, a gloomy brow, a stern face
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Other vices can be concealed and cherished in secret; anger shows itself openly and appears in the countenance, and the greater it is, the more plainly it boils forth. Do you not see how in all animals certain signs appear before they proceed to mischief, and how their entire bodies put off their usual quiet appearance and stir up their ferocity? Boars foam at the mouth and sharpen their teeth by rubbing them against trees, bulls toss their horns in the air and scatter the sand with blows of their feet
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Next, if you choose to view its results and the mischief that it does, no plague has cost the human race more dear
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: See the foundations of the most celebrated cities hardly now to be discerned; they were ruined by anger. See deserts extending for many miles without an inhabitant: they have been desolated by anger.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: What, if you were to pass from the consideration of those single men against whom anger has broken out to view whole assemblies cut down by the sword, the people butchered by the soldiery let loose upon it, and whole nations condemned to death in one common ruin... as though by men who either freed themselves from our charge or despised our authority?
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Everything of this sort is not anger, but the semblance of anger, like that of boys who want to beat the ground when they have fallen upon it, and who often do not even know why they are angry, but are merely angry without any reason or having received any injury, yet not without some semblance of injury received, or without some wish to exact a penalty for it.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Thus they are deceived by the likeness of blows, and are appeased by the pretended tears of those who deprecate their wrath, and thus an unreal grief is healed by an unreal revenge.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: We must admit, however, that neither wild beasts nor any other creature except man is subject to anger: for, whilst anger is the foe of reason, it nevertheless does not arise in any place where reason cannot dwell. Wild beasts have impulses, fury, cruelty, combativeness: they have not anger any more than they have luxury: yet they indulge in some pleasures with less self-control than human beings.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Dumb creatures have not human feelings, but have certain impulses which resemble them: for if it were not so, if they could feel love and hate, they would likewise be capable of friendship and enmity, of disagreement and agreement. Some traces of these qualities exist even in them, though properly all of them, whether good or bad, belong to the human breast alone.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: To no creature besides man has been given wisdom, foresight, industry, and reflection.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: What anger is has been sufficiently explained. The difference between it and irascibility is evident: it is the same as that between a drunken man and a drunkard; between a frightened man and a coward. It is possible for an angry man not to be irascible; an irascible man may sometimes not be angry. I shall omit the other varieties of anger, which the Greeks distinguish by various names, because we have no distinctive words for them in our language, although we call men bitter and harsh, and also peevish, frantic, clamorous, surly and fierce: all of which are different forms of irascibility.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Let us now enquire whether anger be in accordance with nature, and whether it be useful and worth entertaining in some measure.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: What is more affectionate to others than man? Yet what is more savage against them than anger?
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Mankind is born for mutual assistance, anger for mutual ruin: the former loves society, the latter estrangement.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: The one loves to do good, the other to do harm; the one to help even strangers, the other to attack even its dearest friends.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: The one is ready even to sacrifice itself for the good of others, the other to plunge into peril provided it drags others with it.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Who, then, can be more ignorant of nature than he who classes this cruel and hurtful vice as belonging to her best and most polished work?
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Anger, as we have said, is eager to punish; and that such a desire should exist in man’s peaceful breast is least of all according to his nature; for human life is founded on benefits and harmony and is bound together into an alliance for the common help of all, not by terror, but by love towards one another.
quotes.section: Dialogues › On Anger to Novatus

quotes.text: Much must also be withdrawn into oneself: for a well-composed conversation of differences disturbs and renews the affections, and infuriates whatever is weak in the mind and has not been cared for... Loneliness will cure the hatred of the crowd, the boredom of solitude will be cured by the crowd. ... A certain dullness and languor of the mind is born from constant toil. ...Nor would the desire of men so much tend to this, unless play and fun had a kind of natural voluptuousness. The frequent use of which will relieve all the weight of the soul and all the vigor. For sleep is also necessary for refreshment, but if you continue it day and night, death will result.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

quotes.text: The mind must be indulged, and leisure must be given from time to time, which is the place of food and strength.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

quotes.text: To roam in open walks, that the soul may increase and lift itself up in the free air and with much spirit; sometimes travel and a change of country will give vigor, and marriage and more liberal drink. Sometimes even to the point of drunkenness, not that it drowns us, but that it depresses us: for it washes away cares and moves the mind from below, and, as with certain diseases, so it heals sadness.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

quotes.text: You have, dearest Serene, things that can protect tranquility, things that restore it, things that resist creeping escapes. Be it known, however, that none of these things is sufficient for those who hold a feeble matter, unless a constant concern surrounds the slipping mind.
quotes.section: Dialogues › Dialogi de Tranquillitate Animi (Concerning Peace of Mind)

quotes.text: Nothing lasts forever, few things even last for long: all are susceptible of decay in one way or another; moreover all that begins also ends.
quotes.section: Other works

quotes.text: A great fortune is a great slavery.
quotes.section: Other works
quotes.cite: From Ad Polybium De Consolatione (Of Consolation, To Polybius), chap. VI, line 5

quotes.text: Growth is slow but collapse is rapid.
quotes.section: Other works

quotes.text: It would be some consolation for the feebleness of ourselves and our works, if all things should perish as slowly as they come into being; but as it is, increases are of sluggish growth, but the way to ruin is rapid.
quotes.section: Other works
